The topological features of a space have profound effects on it. This is reflected in the homology and cohomology invariants. The Hodge Conjecture focuses on projective complex spaces because these are the most interesting examples; indeed, Hodge lists of manifolds other than the projective complex spaces are easily calculated. Hodge formulated his conjecture to unify the understanding of such manifolds and to understand their Hodge lists. The conjecture can be written in detail as follows.
Consider a given algebraically independent K-cycle Z on a projective complex manifold M, meaning Z is a sum of k-dimensional subvarieties of M, not necessarily connected. A cohomology class ω of M is said to be of type (p,q) if it is homogeneous of degree (p+q) in the exterior algebra of M, 0≤p,q≤k and vanishes on all holomorphic p-forms and meromorphic (p-1)-forms. The Hodge Conjecture states: If ω is a cohomology class of type (p,q) for some K-cycle Z on a projective complex manifold M, then there exist rational (p,q)-forms α and β on M such that ω=α-β.

We must clarify our definition of the P versus NP problem itself here. This problem is defined by the existence of additional structure placed on certain classes of mathematical objects. Specifically, the objects in question are algorithms that can be solved given sufficient time and space on a fixed computer, independent of the state of the computer or the distribution of its operating system, etc. From these classes of algorithms and the relationships between them, the computational complexity classes P and NP are defined. It is conjectured that there are certain algorithms that can be solved with polynomial-time algorithms, but cannot be solved with nondeterministic polynomial time algorithms.

The resolution of this conjecture could have profound ramifications for the fields of artificial intelligence, theoretical computer science, mathematics, and philosophy.

Of central concern in analytic number theory is the study of the Riemann zeta function and its distribution of prime numbers. The Riemann zeta function is the analytic continuation of the Dirichlet series
\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{n^s},
which converges when the real part of s is greater than one. Riemann found a formula for the number of primes less than a real number x. The formula is of the form
\int_0^x \frac{1}{\log t}\,dt - \frac{1}{2\log x} + \int_x^\infty \frac{1}{t^{s+1}\log t}\,dt + \frac{1}{\pi}\int_0^\infty \frac{1}{t^s\sqrt{t}}\frac{\sin(\pi t)}{e^{2\pi t}-1}\,dt
where \Re(s) > 1. Riemann then showed that the zeta function could be defined for all complex numbers s not equal to −1, by the formula
\frac{1}{\Gamma(s)} \int_0^\infty \frac{x^{s-1}}{e^x-1}\, dx,
where
\Gamma(s)
is the gamma function. This result is known as the functional equation of the zeta function. The first term on the right hand side is the usual definition of the zeta function. The remaining terms are the correction term and the error term that interpolates the sum over primes with the analytic continuation of the sum over all natural numbers. The reason for these corrections is that the definition of the zeta function is special at the point s = 1. This is because the gamma function has simple poles at the non-positive integers. The gamma function is defined as

\Gamma(s)=\int_0^\infty t^{s-1} e^{-t} \, dt
for \Re(s) > 0
and

\Gamma(n)=(n-1)!
for n = 1, 2, ...

The Hodge conjecture addresses the simultaneous homology and cohomology of certain kinds of complex manifolds. Homology and cohomology are algebro-geometric invariants. This in turn leads to the presence of topological features, such as nontrivial branches.

These algebro-geometric invariants have applications in fluid dynamics, specifically in fluid turbulence. In the limit of incompressible, inviscid flow of an ideal gas, the Navier-Stokes equations can be reduced to a complex Monge-Ampere equation. This in turn is a consequence of the Hodge conjugation of the underlying Riemannian metric.듕גניםuser

Poincaré is excluded because it was already solved at the forecast date.

Forecast event: a correct complete solution to at least one of these problems, meeting its original Clay Mathematics Institute mathematical formulation, is first publicly available, and AI has contributed an identifiable new mathematical argument or proof step incorporated into that solution. Substantive human-AI collaboration qualifies. Correctness may be established by later validation; a Clay prize need not be awarded by the deadline. Partial progress alone does not qualify. Give one probability for at least one qualifying solution by each deadline; do not give separate probabilities for individual problems.

For each deadline, state your probability that this event will have occurred by then. The deadlines are December 31 of 2026, 2030, 2035, 2040, and 2050. Probabilities must be numbers between 0 and 1 inclusive, nondecreasing with the deadline. Account for the possibility the event never occurs. Give your own best probability estimates despite uncertainty. Return only one JSON object with exactly the keys "2026", "2030", "2035", "2040", and "2050" and their numerical probabilities, with no markdown or explanation.<|im_end|>
